newsitem.title: USA: Steady Fed sparks criticism from Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Steady Fed sparks criticism from Wall Street.

text.p: Federal Reserve inflation fighters held their fire on Tuesday by leaving U.S. interest rates unchanged, buoying U.S. asset markets but sparking criticism from some economists on Wall Street.

"It's not like (Fed chief Alan) Greenspan is bowing to political pressures, but the risk of the Fed being wrong here is dangerous," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Inc.

Others were less sure political pressure from Washington played no role in Greenspan's decision to leave rates steady after the Fed's much-maligned rise of 25 basis points in the federal funds rate on March 25.

"The Fed never likes to be seen as being unduly influenced, much less captive, to political pressures, but with (this) inaction, there is a risk the markets would come to believe that," said Wayne Ayers, chief economist at the Bank of Boston.

Some economists said that Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) members were duped by April's relatively soft economic data which signalled a slowdown from the first quarter's booming rate of economic growth.

"They have taken the head-fake of the most recent data and that will significantly increase the odds of them having to move 50 (basis points higher) at the next meeting," said Steven Wood, managing director at BancAmerica Inc.

But under no circumstances was Greenspan going to emerge from Tuesday's meeting without hearing cries of protest. The chorus of naysayers would have been even louder had FOMC members raised rates, market experts said.
"It is, in a way, a no-win situation for Greenspan and he bites the bullet either way," Ayers said.
The complexity of Greenspan's dilemma was evidenced by Wall Street's inability to reach a consensus on the appropriate policy outcome from the FOMC.
According to pre-meeting polls, analysts were almost equally divided on the need for monetary authorities to raise rates for a second time to ward off future inflation.

While recent price data has been soft, an extremely low 4.9 percent unemployment rate in April combined with booming economic growth of 5.6 percent in the first quarter has economists concerned that price pressures are brewing.
"You can make arguments very easily for both a move and no move," Sanwa's Strauss said.

However, Greenspan should find support on Capitol Hill where politicians openly protested his decision last March to corral inflation by raising rates at the possible expense of economic growth and jobs.

A U.S. Treasuries dealer said Greenspan has a "reservoir of goodwill" in the marketplace which will help silence critics, adding that economic data releases over the next two months should clarify the nation's economic direction and give Greenspan "something to hang his hat on" at the next policy meeting in July.

"I don't think it is political pressure. I think Greenspan needs to have all his ducks lined up to justify a move without any second-guessing," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan.
